name: TypeScript
description: Structural typing, narrowing, generics and the type-level tools that make large codebases tractable.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What TypeScript is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is TypeScript, and why do teams use it?
cards.answer: JavaScript with static types added. You annotate (or let the compiler infer) the types of values, and the TypeScript compiler reports mistakes — a typo'd property, a missing argument, a possible `undefined` — before the code ever runs.
cards.explanation: Every valid JavaScript program is (almost always) valid TypeScript, so it can be adopted gradually. The payoff grows with codebase size: editors can autocomplete and refactor safely because they know what every value is.

resources.title: TypeScript Handbook — TypeScript for the new programmer

cards.prompt: Who makes TypeScript, and when did it appear?
cards.answer: Microsoft, first released in 2012. Its lead architect is Anders Hejlsberg, who also designed C# (and Turbo Pascal and Delphi before that).
cards.explanation: TypeScript is open source and tracks JavaScript closely: it adopts new ECMAScript features as they are standardised rather than inventing its own runtime features, so its main contribution is the type system layered on top.

cards.prompt: How does TypeScript code run, given that browsers and Node.js run JavaScript?
cards.answer: It is compiled (transpiled) to plain JavaScript — by `tsc`, or by fast tools such as esbuild or swc — and the JavaScript is what runs. The types are erased: none of them exist at run time.
cards.explanation: Type erasure means TypeScript cannot check data arriving at run time (JSON from an API, user input); you validate that with a library such as Zod. Recent Node.js versions can run `.ts` files directly by stripping the type annotations, but no type checking happens on that path.

cards.prompt: What does a minimal TypeScript program look like?
cards.answer: JavaScript plus an optional type annotation. `: string` declares the variable's type; the compiler would reject assigning a number to it.
cards.explanation: You rarely need to annotate everything: TypeScript infers types from values, so `const greeting = "Hello"` is already known to be a string. Annotations are most useful on function parameters and public APIs.

cards.prompt: TypeScript vs JavaScript
cards.answer: TypeScript adds a compile-time type checker and a build step; JavaScript runs directly. At run time they are the same language.

right.title: JavaScript
points: Errors found when the line executes

cards.explanation: Small scripts gain little from TypeScript; large, long-lived codebases with many contributors gain a lot. Many libraries ship type definitions so even JavaScript projects get autocomplete from them.

resources.title: TypeScript Handbook — TypeScript for JavaScript programmers

cards.prompt: What is `tsconfig.json`, and what does `"strict": true` do?
cards.answer: `tsconfig.json` marks a TypeScript project and holds its compiler options. `strict` switches on the full set of strict checks — most importantly `strictNullChecks` and `noImplicitAny` — and is the recommended default for new code.
cards.explanation: Without strict null checks every type silently includes `null` and `undefined`, which hides the most common run-time crash in JavaScript. Turning strict mode on later in a large codebase is painful, so start with it on.

modules.name: Type System Foundations
modules.description: What TypeScript actually checks, and the mental model behind its answers.

cards.prompt: Is TypeScript's type system nominal or structural?
cards.answer: Structural. Compatibility is decided by shape, not by declared name or inheritance — if it has the required members with compatible types, it fits.
cards.explanation: Two unrelated interfaces with identical members are interchangeable. When you need nominal behaviour (an `OrderId` that a plain string cannot satisfy) you brand the type: `type OrderId = string & { readonly __brand: unique symbol }`.

cards.prompt: `any` vs `unknown`
cards.answer: `any` disables checking; `unknown` accepts anything but forbids use until narrowed.

right.title: unknown
points: Accepts any value on the way in
Nothing can be done with it before narrowing
The correct type for JSON, catch clauses, IPC

cards.explanation: `unknown` is the type-safe top type. Use it at every boundary where data arrives from outside the program, then validate. Every `any` is a hole where the compiler stops helping — and holes propagate.

cards.prompt: `type` alias vs `interface`
cards.answer: Interfaces declare object shapes and merge across declarations; type aliases name any type at all, including unions and mapped types.

left.title: interface
points: Slightly better error messages in places

right.title: type
points: Cannot be reopened — no accidental merging
Required for anything type-level and clever

cards.explanation: A practical rule: interfaces for public object contracts you may want others to augment, type aliases for everything else. Never mix both for the same concept in one codebase.

resources.title: TypeScript Handbook — Interfaces vs type aliases

cards.prompt: Which constructs narrow a union type in TypeScript?
cards.answer: `typeof`, `instanceof`, truthiness checks, equality against literals, the `in` operator, discriminated-union switches, and user-defined type predicates (`x is Foo`).
cards.explanation: Control-flow analysis tracks the narrowed type per branch. Discriminated unions — a shared literal `kind` field — are the most robust option because adding a variant produces an exhaustiveness error where you handle them, if you assign the default branch to `never`.

cards.prompt: What does the compiler do when a new variant is added to `Shape` but not to the switch?
cards.answer: It errors at the `never` assignment: the new variant is not assignable to `never`, pointing straight at the unhandled case.
cards.explanation: This is the exhaustiveness check. Without it, a missing case silently falls through at runtime. With it, every place that switches on the union fails to compile the moment the union grows — turning a whole class of bug into a compile error.

cards.prompt: Why does this fail at runtime?
cards.answer: Interfaces are erased at compile time — there is no `User` value at runtime to use with `instanceof`. Check the shape manually, or validate with a schema library such as Zod.
cards.explanation: TypeScript types vanish entirely in the emitted JavaScript. Anything that must exist at runtime — validation, discriminants, reflection — has to be written as real code or generated from a schema that also produces the type.

modules.name: Generics & Type-Level Programming
modules.description: Constraints, inference, conditional and mapped types, and the utility types worth memorising.

cards.prompt: To require that a generic parameter has a `length`, write `function f<T ___ { length: number }>(x: T)`.
cards.answer: extends
cards.explanation: `extends` constrains a type parameter — read it as 'is assignable to'. Constraints let you use members inside the function while preserving the caller's exact type in the return, which a plain `{ length: number }` parameter would throw away.

cards.prompt: What do `Partial`, `Required`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`, `ReturnType` and `Awaited` do?
cards.answer: Partial makes all properties optional; Required removes optionality; Pick selects keys; Omit removes keys; Record builds a map type from keys to values; ReturnType extracts a function's return type; Awaited unwraps a promise.
cards.explanation: These are ordinary types built from mapped and conditional types — nothing magic. Deriving types (`Omit<User, 'password'>`) instead of re-declaring them keeps the two in sync forever, which is the entire point of a structural type system.

cards.prompt: What is `Unwrap<Promise<string[]>>`?
cards.answer: `A` is `string[]` and `B` is `number`.
cards.explanation: `infer` declares a type variable inside a conditional type and binds it by pattern matching. If the pattern does not match, the false branch returns the input unchanged. This is the mechanism behind `ReturnType`, `Parameters` and `Awaited`.

cards.prompt: What does the `satisfies` operator give you that a type annotation does not?
cards.answer: It checks the value against a type **without** widening the inferred type — you keep the narrow literal inference and still get the constraint checked.
cards.explanation: `const config: Record<string, string> = {...}` loses the specific keys. `const config = {...} satisfies Record<string, string>` validates the shape but leaves `config` with its exact literal key set, so lookups stay type-safe.

cards.prompt: You inherit a TypeScript codebase with `strict: false`. What do you turn on, and in what order?
cards.answer: Enable `strict` family flags incrementally: `noImplicitAny` first, then `strictNullChecks` (the big one), then the rest — fixing each wave before moving on.
cards.explanation: `strictNullChecks` is where the real defect-finding happens: without it, `null` and `undefined` inhabit every type and the compiler cannot warn you. Migrate directory by directory if needed, and add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` once the basics are clean.

cards.prompt: `enum` vs a union of string literals
cards.answer: Enums emit runtime code and are nominal-ish; literal unions are pure types with zero runtime cost.

left.title: enum Status { ... }
points: Numeric enums still accept any `number` variable — loosely checked
Awkward across module and bundler boundaries; unsupported by type-stripping runtimes

right.title: type Status = 'a' | 'b'
points: Values are plain strings, easy to log and serialise
Pair with `as const` objects when you need a value list

cards.explanation: Most modern codebases prefer literal unions plus an `as const` object when a runtime list is required. It serialises naturally, works across bundlers, and never surprises anyone reading the emitted JavaScript.

modules.name: Type Operators & Modelling
modules.description: keyof, typeof, indexed and mapped types, literal inference and modelling data precisely.

cards.prompt: What are the types `Keys` and `Level`?
cards.answer: `Keys` is `'debug' | 'info' | 'error'` and `Level` is `0 | 1 | 2`.
cards.explanation: `typeof` lifts a value into the type world, `keyof` produces the union of an object type's keys, and indexed access `T[K]` looks up property types. `as const` keeps the literal values (and makes them readonly) instead of widening to `number`. Deriving types from one runtime object keeps both in sync forever.

cards.prompt: What is a mapped type, and how would you write `Readonly<T>` yourself?
cards.answer: `type MyReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };` — a mapped type iterates over a union of keys and produces a property for each. Modifiers can be added or removed with `+`/`-` (`-?` removes optionality, as `Required` does).
cards.explanation: Key remapping with `as` lets you rename or filter keys: `{ [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] }` builds getter names. Most built-in utility types are one-line mapped or conditional types.

cards.prompt: What is the type `Route`?
cards.answer: `'GET /users' | 'GET /orders' | 'POST /users' | 'POST /orders'`
cards.explanation: Template literal types distribute over unions, producing every combination. Combined with `infer` they can also parse strings at the type level — for example extracting `:id` parameters from a route pattern — which is how typed routers and event emitters work.

cards.prompt: Union (`A | B`) vs intersection (`A & B`)
cards.answer: A union value is one of the types, so you may only use members common to all until you narrow. An intersection value is all of the types at once, so it has every member.

left.title: A | B (union)
points: Narrow with typeof, in, or a discriminant

right.title: A & B (intersection)
points: All members of both are accessible

cards.explanation: The names feel backwards at first: a union of object types has *fewer* usable properties, an intersection has *more*. Intersections of incompatible primitives (`string & number`) collapse to `never`, which is exactly what makes branding work when combined with an object tag.

resources.title: TypeScript Handbook — Everyday types — union types

cards.prompt: What does `readonly` guarantee, and what does it not?
cards.answer: It is a compile-time check that prevents assignment through that reference: `readonly` properties, `ReadonlyArray<T>` / `readonly T[]`, and `as const` for deep literal inference. It emits nothing, so it does not freeze the object at runtime.
cards.explanation: Readonly is shallow for properties and not a guarantee of immutability: another reference typed as mutable can still change the object. Accept `readonly T[]` in function parameters — it documents that you will not mutate the caller's array and accepts both mutable and readonly arrays.

resources.title: TypeScript Handbook — Object types — readonly properties

cards.prompt: Why is this unsafe, and what should replace it?
cards.answer: `as User` is an assertion: it tells the compiler to trust you and checks nothing at runtime, so malformed JSON flows through typed as `User`. Parse into `unknown` and validate — with a schema library such as Zod, or a type guard that actually checks the fields.
cards.explanation: Assertions (`as`) and non-null assertions (`!`) are the escape hatches that most often hide real bugs. A type predicate `(x): x is User` is only as correct as its body, so schema validators that derive the type from the runtime check are the safest option at trust boundaries.

resources.title: TypeScript Handbook — Everyday types — type assertions

cards.prompt: This compiles under `strict` but crashes at runtime. Why, and which flag catches it?
cards.answer: Index access on arrays and records is typed as `T`, not `T | undefined`, so the compiler assumes `names[5]` exists. Enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` types it as `string | undefined`, forcing a check before `.toUpperCase()`.
cards.explanation: This flag is not part of `strict` because it is noisy in loops, but it catches a real class of crash — out-of-range indexes and missing record keys. Iterating with `for...of` or `.map` avoids the noise, because those give defined elements.

cards.prompt: When should you use function overloads, and what is the usual alternative?
cards.answer: Overloads declare several call signatures above one implementation, for when the return type depends on the argument type in ways a single signature cannot express. The implementation signature itself is not callable from outside.
cards.explanation: Prefer a union parameter or a generic where possible — overloads are checked only against the implementation's looser signature, so it is easy to lie. A conditional return type or a discriminated options object is often clearer than three overloads.

resources.title: TypeScript Handbook — More on functions — overloads

cards.prompt: `object` vs `{}` vs `unknown`
cards.answer: `unknown` accepts every value; `{}` accepts every value except `null` and `undefined` (primitives included); `object` accepts only non-primitive values.

left.title: unknown / {}
points: `unknown`: literally anything, must narrow to use
Neither lets you read properties freely

right.title: object
points: Still needs narrowing to read keys

cards.explanation: `{}` does not mean "empty object" — `const x: {} = 42` compiles. Use `Record<string, never>` for a genuinely empty object, `object` for "any non-primitive", and `unknown` for untyped input you will narrow.

modules.name: Compiler, Modules & Declarations
modules.description: tsconfig, module resolution, declaration files, type-only imports and how TypeScript meets the runtime.

cards.prompt: What is a `.d.ts` file, and where do types for untyped packages come from?
cards.answer: A declaration file containing only types — no implementation — describing JavaScript that exists elsewhere. Libraries ship their own (`"types"` in package.json); for untyped packages the community publishes them as `@types/<name>` from DefinitelyTyped.
cards.explanation: You can write `declare module "legacy-lib";` as a stopgap (everything becomes `any`) or author proper declarations. `declare global` augments global types, and interface declaration merging extends third-party types such as a framework's request object.

cards.prompt: What do `import type` and `verbatimModuleSyntax` solve?
cards.answer: `import type { User }` is guaranteed to be erased, so no runtime import of the module remains. `verbatimModuleSyntax` makes the rule explicit: imports without `type` are kept as written, imports with `type` are dropped — no guessing by the compiler.
cards.explanation: Single-file transpilers (esbuild, SWC, Babel, Node type stripping) compile one file at a time and cannot know whether an imported name is only a type. Marking type imports explicitly keeps their output correct and avoids accidental side-effect imports and circular-dependency surprises.

cards.prompt: A package works at runtime but TypeScript says it cannot find its types, or the reverse. What is the likely cause and fix?
cards.answer: A mismatch between how TypeScript resolves modules and how your runtime or bundler does. Set `module`/`moduleResolution` to match reality: `nodenext` for code run directly by Node (which honours `exports` and requires file extensions in ESM), or `bundler` for code consumed by Vite, webpack or esbuild.
cards.explanation: The legacy `node` (node10) resolution ignores package.json `exports`, so it disagrees with modern packages. Getting this setting right removes most "works in tests, fails in build" import errors.

cards.prompt: `tsc` type-checking vs fast transpilers (esbuild, SWC, Node type stripping)
cards.answer: `tsc` type-checks the whole program and can emit JavaScript; fast transpilers only strip types, file by file, without checking anything.

right.title: esbuild / SWC / Node
points: One file at a time: needs `isolatedModules`
Used by bundlers and dev servers

cards.explanation: The standard setup splits the jobs: a fast transpiler in the dev server and build, plus `tsc --noEmit` in CI and the editor for checking. Features that need type information to emit (enums, namespaces, parameter properties) are why `erasableSyntaxOnly` exists for type-stripping runtimes.

cards.prompt: What is the inferred type of `a` and `b`?
cards.answer: `a` is `Box<number>` (inferred from the argument) and `b` is `Box<string>` (the default, because nothing could be inferred).
cards.explanation: Type parameters are inferred from arguments when possible, fall back to their default when not, and to their constraint when there is no default. Put inferable parameters first and defaulted ones last. `NoInfer<T>` (5.4) stops an argument from influencing inference when it should only be checked against it.

cards.prompt: Why does TypeScript let you assign `Dog[]` to `Animal[]`, and why is that unsound?
cards.answer: Arrays (and method parameters) are checked covariantly for convenience. But a mutable `Animal[]` alias lets you push a `Cat` into what is really a `Dog[]`, so the original array now holds a cat.
cards.explanation: TypeScript deliberately trades soundness for ergonomics in a few places: array covariance, method parameter bivariance, and `any`. `strictFunctionTypes` makes function-typed properties contravariant in their parameters, and `readonly` arrays are safely covariant — another reason to accept `readonly T[]`.
